name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
title: Long-Term Digital Preservation
answer: Long-term digital preservation in research data and repositories concerns keeping digital objects readable, usable, and authentic beyond the life of the software, hardware, and institutions that created them. It covers research datasets, code, documentation, metadata, and the repository systems that hold them. The goal is not backup or short-term storage but sustained access over decades, often with no clear end date. Practitioners work with file formats, checksums, persistent identifiers, and preservation metadata.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Long-term digital preservation in research data and repositories concerns keeping digital objects readable, usable, and authentic beyond the life of the software, hardware, and institutions that created them. It covers research datasets, code, documentation, metadata, and the repository systems that hold them. The goal is not backup or short-term storage but sustained access over decades, often with no clear end date. Practitioners work with file formats, checksums, persistent identifiers, and preservation metadata.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Preservation infrastructure typically includes repository software, storage layers with geographic replication, and fixity checking. Storage may span tape, disk, and cloud object stores, with multiple copies held by different organisations. Persistent identifiers such as DOIs and Handles point to preserved objects, while registries track formats and software environments. The infrastructure must survive changes in institutional funding and technical staff.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through active curation rather than passive storage. Files are normalised to open, well-documented formats, and significant properties are recorded so future users know what must be preserved. Checksums are generated and verified on a schedule to detect bit rot or accidental change. Emulation and migration are two main strategies: either recreate the original computing environment or convert content to newer formats before the old one becomes unusable. Metadata standards such as PREMIS record events, agents, and rights over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in long-term preservation centre on ownership, access conditions, and the chain of custody. Repositories must document who deposited an object, what permissions apply, and whether access can change over time. Risk includes format obsolescence, media failure, organisational loss, and legal uncertainty about re-use. Provenance is maintained through audit trails and preservation metadata, so a future user can see what transformations an object has undergone. Trusted digital repository certification, such as CoreTrustSeal, provides a recognised benchmark but does not remove the need for ongoing review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward greater automation in format identification, risk assessment, and migration planning. Machine learning is being explored to classify file types, predict obsolescence, and summarise preservation metadata, though human review remains central. Repositories are also testing active preservation of software and computational environments, not just static files. The long-term challenge is to preserve enough context for future researchers to understand and re-run work without relying on any single vendor or platform.
